subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: At a cholinergic synapse, the arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic membrane triggers:
options: Reuptake of acetylcholine
Influx of potassium ions
Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, causing vesicles to fuse and release acetylcholine
Direct flow of current across the cleft
questions.explain: Depolarisation opens Ca2+ channels; calcium influx causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.

questions.q: In the second messenger model of glucagon action, the binding of glucagon to its receptor leads to:
options: Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
Insulin being released by exocytosis
Activation of adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, which activates protein kinase A
Direct entry of glucagon into the cell to activate enzymes
questions.explain: Glucagon activates adenylate cyclase, producing cAMP as a second messenger that activates protein kinase A to trigger glycogenolysis.

questions.q: The role of calcium ions in muscle contraction is to:
options: Break the cross-bridges between actin and myosin
Provide the energy for the power stroke
Bind to troponin, moving tropomyosin to expose the myosin-binding sites on actin
Resynthesise ATP from ADP
questions.explain: Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin, shifting tropomyosin to uncover actin binding sites so cross-bridges can form.

questions.q: The counter-current multiplier in the loop of Henle works because:
options: The descending limb actively pumps in water
Both limbs are equally permeable to water and ions
The ascending limb is permeable to water but not ions
The ascending limb actively pumps out sodium ions, creating a high solute concentration (low water potential) in the medulla
questions.explain: Active removal of Na+ from the impermeable-to-water ascending limb builds a medullary solute gradient that draws water out of the descending limb and collecting duct.

questions.q: When the water potential of the blood falls, ADH is released and causes:
options: The loop of Henle to pump out more sodium
More aquaporins to be inserted into the collecting duct, increasing water reabsorption
Less water to be reabsorbed, producing dilute urine
Increased filtration at the glomerulus
questions.explain: ADH makes the collecting duct walls more permeable by inserting aquaporins, so more water is reabsorbed and concentrated urine is produced.

questions.q: The repolarisation phase of an action potential is brought about by:
options: Calcium ions entering the axon
The sodium-potassium pump alone
Potassium channels opening so K+ diffuses out of the axon
Sodium channels opening
questions.explain: Voltage-gated K+ channels open and K+ leaves the axon, restoring the negative internal potential (repolarisation).

questions.q: Type 1 diabetes differs from type 2 in that:
options: Type 1 is usually treated by diet and exercise alone
Type 1 results from autoimmune destruction of beta cells so little or no insulin is produced
Type 1 is caused by target cells losing responsiveness to insulin
Type 1 has a later onset and is linked to obesity
questions.explain: In type 1 the immune system destroys insulin-secreting beta cells, whereas type 2 involves reduced insulin sensitivity of target cells.

questions.q: Ultrafiltration in the renal glomerulus occurs because:
options: The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, lowering pressure
High hydrostatic blood pressure forces small molecules through the basement membrane, which acts as a filter
Active transport pushes plasma into the Bowman's capsule
Plasma proteins are actively secreted into the filtrate
questions.explain: High pressure (helped by a narrower efferent arteriole) forces water and small solutes through the basement membrane, which holds back proteins and cells.

questions.q: Glucagon raises blood glucose principally by stimulating:
options: Glycogenesis and glucose uptake
Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver
Insulin secretion from beta cells
The conversion of glucose to fat
questions.explain: Glucagon promotes breakdown of glycogen (glycogenolysis) and synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (gluconeogenesis) in the liver.

questions.q: Negative feedback in homeostasis acts to:
options: Maintain a constant rate of change
Switch off all hormone secretion permanently
Amplify a deviation from the set point
Reverse a change and return a factor toward its set point
questions.explain: Negative feedback detects a deviation and triggers responses that oppose it, restoring the internal environment toward the set point.

questions.q: In the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction shortens the sarcomere because:
options: Calcium ions are pumped out of the sarcoplasm
The actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten
Myosin heads form cross-bridges and pull the actin filaments past the myosin toward the centre
The H zone widens as filaments slide apart
questions.explain: Myosin heads bind actin and, powered by ATP, pull the thin filaments inward so the sarcomere shortens while filament lengths stay the same.

questions.q: In the proximal convoluted tubule, glucose is reabsorbed by:
options: Co-transport with sodium ions across the apical membrane
Pinocytosis of the filtrate
Osmosis following the water
Simple diffusion through the basement membrane
questions.explain: Glucose is reabsorbed by sodium-glucose co-transport, the Na+ gradient being maintained by Na+/K+ pumps on the basolateral membrane.
